articles.title: Keeping London's canal boats afloat during summer drought
articles.summary: Locks on the Grand Union canal in are closed at night in hopes of managing water levels downstream.
articles.body:
Drought conditions in the capital mean that London's waterways are being more actively managed to maintain water levels.

In west London on the Grand Union Canal, the gates of six locks known as the Hanwell Flight have been locked up at night with their paddles shut to prevent misuse that impacts the canal downstream.

Colin Beesley, waterway operative at Canal and River Trust, described the situation as "unprecedented", adding: "It's been one of the driest summers we've ever seen and of course there's been virtually no rain.

"Because this drought has been extending for so long, we've made the decision to lock this flight of locks overnight."

Additionally, all of the lock gates have been "ashed up", a traditional method of sealing gaps between planks in lock gates with coal dust to hold water in.

The action on the Hanwell Flight has helped maintain water levels at the "Long Pound", a 27 mile (43.4km) lock-free stretch which encompasses the Grand Union Main Line, Paddington Arm and Regent's Canal all the way to Camden.

In east London, closures are also helping to manage the water levels.

Charlotte Wood, head of operations at the Canal and River Trust, explained that they have closed the Hertford Union Canal, a 1.2 mile (2km) long stretch of water that acts as a short-cut from the Regent's Canal to the River Lee, avoiding the River Thames.

Wood said the "non-critical" route near Victoria Park was closed so that water coming in from west London from the Hanwell Flight area and beyond went into central London.

"We're keeping the Regent's Canal open for as long as possible for our boats to move and to keep afloat," she added.

In Hanwell, boats are still allowed to travel through the canal during the day, but for boaters like Paul Findlay, the drought has made things much more challenging.

"It's kind of the new normal really," he said. "You have to get used to it in the summer months.

"It needs careful management by both the boaters and the people looking after the canals.

"If we work together we can help keep it as good as it can be."

Nicholas Jones, area operations manager at the Canal and River Trust, said they were using an app to monitor water levels, and were also keeping a close eye on the weather, adding that he was "deeply desperate" for rain to return to the capital.

"We get hopeful whenever it starts to speckle slightly, but it generally never arrives," he said.

This stretch of the Grand Union Canal has been open since 1794 - all the locks need now is more water to fill them.

articles.title: In 2016, Mark Zuckerberg's wife Priscilla Chan founded a school that was designed to be different; 10 years later and after $125 million funding, Board voted to close it
articles.summary: Tech News News: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerbergâs wife Dr. Priscilla Chan, co-founded The Primary School in East Palo Alto, California in 2016. The school was designed to se.
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerbergâs wife Dr. Priscilla Chan, co-founded The Primary School in East Palo Alto, California in 2016. The school was designed to serve the low-income families. The tuition-free private school aimed to support the âwhole childâ through wraparound services such as dental checkups, wellness coaching, and early-intervention screenings. For more than ten years the school received more than $125 million from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI). However, despite the strong support services and community engagement, academic performance often fell short of state norms, complicating efforts to replicate the model in public and charter schools. A report by Wall Street Journal revealed that despite all these efforts the school shut its doors this past June after a decade of operation.Why the board voted to close school founded by Priscilla ChanThe Primary School's board voted unanimously in April 2025 to close the school after learning that CZI would not continue funding it beyond the 2025-26 academic year, according to people familiar with the situation. Board president Jean-Claude Brizard said he had presented CZI with several options for the school's future before the vote, including winding the school down gradually, and said the board would not have voted to close without alignment from its primary funder. A CZI spokesperson said the decision to close ultimately rested with the school's board, and that the organization's focus had been on the school's academic results rather than cost.The closure reflects a broader shift within CZI, which has moved its philanthropic focus away from social issues and toward scientific research in recent years.A mixed academic recordBy some measures, the Primary School's academic performance fell short of both state benchmarks and its own leadership's expectations, complicating efforts to eventually replicate its model in public and charter schools elsewhere. A Stanford University report found that in spring 2025, 14% of local third-grade-and-above students exceeded state literacy standards, compared to 26% at the Primary School itself and 47% statewide. Still, the school said its eighth-grade students, many of whom had attended for a decade, demonstrated above 50% grade-level proficiency in their final year, and a founding staff member said students showed steady academic progress after the pandemic, alongside improvements in wellbeing and socio-emotional skills. Around 85% of Primary School students completed their annual well-child visit, compared to 55% of children on Medicaid in the county.Impact on familiesAround 540 children were enrolled across the two campuses of the Primary School. As per the WSJ report, Mele Fakapelea, whose daughter Telesia won a lottery spot in the school's founding class before Fakapelea enrolled four younger children as well, described it as "a godsend school," and said losing its support system felt devastating. On the other hand, Angelica Cardenas, whose 3-year-old daughter and five nieces and nephews were enrolled, said she learned about the closure through the news rather than directly from the school, arguing that families should have been told sooner if funding was going to end. After the shut down of the Primary School founded by Priscilla Chan, the students will be absorbed in the Ravenswood City Elementary School District. The school is also preparing for an enrollment surge and renovating a campus to avoid placing students in portable trailers.What CZI is providing as the school winds downCZI pledged $50 million when the closure was announced, covering the remaining balance of the school's lease with the district and supporting local organizations to continue offering some services. The organization also contributed $3.6 million toward education savings accounts for affected families: $10,000 per elementary student, $2,500 per preschooler, and $1,000 for children in early-childhood education programs.Priscilla Chan's hands-on roleChan served as the Primary School's co-founder and board chair for about eight years, until 2023, with CZI functioning as its main funder throughout. According to CZI, having a single major backer indefinitely was never the intended long-term model; the goal had been a school that could eventually be sustained primarily through public investment, and the school reportedly tried to keep its per-pupil spending in line with typical public school levels. Brizard said Chan actively lobbied her network to bring in additional funding sources, though attracting outside donors proved difficult given the perception of a school already backed by one of the world's wealthiest individuals.Chan was known to be candid about her frustration with the school's academic outcomes, telling the Journal last year that results weren't where anyone would have wanted them to be. Brizard said the timing of CZI's broader strategic shift, which staff were told about in early 2025 shortly after Zuckerberg and Chan attended President Trump's inauguration, and the board's subsequent vote to close was coincidental; CZI said there was no evidence the inauguration had influenced the board's decision.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Southampton AI uncovers hidden clues in breast cancer
articles.summary: The findings could help doctors identify high-risk patients and develop more targeted treatments.
articles.body:
Researchers have developed an AI tool that reveals previously unseen patterns inside breast cancers.

A University of Southampton team, working with the city's hospital, used the technology to analyse more than 330,000 cells from 127 patients.

The findings could help doctors identify high-risk patients and develop more targeted treatments.

Leading the research, the university's Dr Salah Elias, said: "This opens the door to developing new biomarkers and, ultimately, more personalised treatment strategies."

The study found two different types of changes inside cancer cells that had previously been treated as the same thing.

One type involved cells developing too many centrosomes, which help cells divide properly. The other involved centrosomes becoming unusually large.

Researchers discovered the two changes could appear in different parts of the same tumour and may play different roles in how cancers develop.

The team created an AI platform, called CenSegNet, to examine tumour samples with "unprecedented speed and precision".

Centrosomes act as the cell's organising centres, helping cells divide and maintain their structure. When they become abnormal, cells can build up genetic mistakes, which are commonly seen in cancer.

The researchers found tumours with higher numbers of enlarged centrosomes were more likely to have features linked to more aggressive disease.

These included higher tumour grade, cancer that had spread to nearby lymph nodes and certain genetic changes.

The study also found patients with fewer enlarged centrosomes in the centre of their tumours tended to have better overall survival.

Elias, said: "For more than a century, centrosome abnormalities have been recognised as a hallmark of cancer, but studying them in patient tissues has been extremely challenging.

"CenSegNet allows us to analyse these defects at single-cell resolution across entire tumours and uncover patterns that were previously impossible to see."

Researchers say the technology could eventually help doctors better understand which cancers are more likely to grow, spread or resist treatment.

It could also help scientists develop more personalised treatments by identifying tumours with specific weaknesses that could be targeted with new drugs.

While the technology is not yet ready for routine use in hospitals, the team has also shown it can be used on tissue samples from other parts of the body, including the kidney, colon and appendix.

CenSegNet is available free of charge as open-source software, allowing researchers around the world to use and study the technology.

articles.summary: Europe News: Indian company BLS International has been drawn into a Spanish National Court investigation with links to alleged visa fraud network at Spainâs consul.
articles.body: Indian company BLS International has been drawn into a Spanish National Court investigation with links to alleged visa fraud network at Spainâs consulate in Algiers. The allegations have been denied by the firm.The probe, led by Judge MarÃ­a TardÃ³n, was expanded to examine the role of companies handling visa appointments and document processing, including BLS, which is contracted by Spainâs Foreign Ministry, as reported by Spanish news outlet The Objective.However, BLS International issued a statement rejecting any involvement in the alleged irregularities. "There is no evidence establishing any wrongdoing by BLS International or its employees in relation to the issuance of visas. BLS Internationalâs role is strictly administrative and is carried out in accordance with the requirements prescribed by the competent authorities," said the firm."All decisions relating to the processing and issuance or refusal of visas rest solely with the relevant diplomatic and consular authorities. BLS International remains committed to the highest standards of integrity, transparency, compliance and service delivery, and to its role as a trusted service partner to governments and citizens across the world," it added.The investigation began following âofficial communicationsâ from the Spanish Embassy in Algeria, which alerted authorities to a network allegedly âprofiting through the fraudulent issuance of Schengen visasâ. articles.title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
articles.summary: Five years after the Talibanâs return, the BBC follows senior figures as the group reshapes the country.
articles.body:
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.

A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.

In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.

"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be hereâ¦ I have taken my decision," she says.

After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.

The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.

In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.

In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.

The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.

The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.

Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule Published 14 August

Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule

Five years of the BBC questioning the Taliban over women and girls' education Published 14 August

Five years of the BBC questioning the Taliban over women and girls' education

Governor Sarhadi says Tuba â not her real name â should stay in the marriage.

"Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour."

"Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.

Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.

Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.

The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".

Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.

Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.

He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.

When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.

Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick messageâ¦ sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.

But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.

He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands.

"Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's lawâ¦ We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."

In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.

Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.

He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul.

"I know all the roads and streets very wellâ¦ we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."

Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.

Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".

Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.

Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.

He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country â and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.

Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn.

"Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."

An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.

Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopenâ¦ seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."

He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."

Audiences in the UK can watch on iPlayer from 17:00 and on Global Eye on BBC Two at 19:00

Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.

Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.

Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.

The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.

He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.

In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.

Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?

"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."

Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.

He says the issue of education for women is "under discussionsâ¦ we need a Sharia-based solution for it".

When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they wantâ¦ they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."

The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.

We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.

Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.

Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.

Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.

His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.

The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics.

"Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."

Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.

Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem.

"I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power.

"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."

"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."

"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."

"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."

Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

articles.title: Hampshire car wash 'worried' about possible business water use ban
articles.summary: Owners of a car wash are "worried" about the impact a water ban could have on its business and customers.
articles.body:
Operators of a car wash have said it will have to "close up" if further drought restrictions are approved.

Klodian Ferati from Pinkmead Car Wash in Botley, Hampshire, is "worried" about the potential impact a Non-Essential Use Ban (NEUB) could have on its staff, jobs and customers if approved.

Southern Water has applied to the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) for a Drought Order and NEUB , which could prevent businesses from using water.

The Environment Agency declared more than half of England in drought, and said as a precautionary measure the ban could be implemented to "protect water supplies and the environment".

Ferati said if it does come into effect the business "would close up completely because without water we can't actually do anything".

Pinkmead Car Wash was set up in 15 years ago, by manager Ferati and his family, because of their love for cars.

He said: "As a family, we love cars. We've always had cars and, you know, loved washing them at home.

"It will impact us a lot, even the business and the workers, because the business has rent to pay, has bills to pay, and the workers, they rely on this job. They have no other income.

"We could still do just the hoovering on the inside of the cars, but most of the customers, they're going to want their cars washed on the outside."

Klodian understands the need for the ban but hopes there can be a solution that means the business doesn't have to close: "We completely understand that Southern Water is short on water.

"But I think it's a great idea to work together and basically just come to a conclusion where we could, you know, use less water than before, and basically just carry on working."

A spokesperson for Southern Water, said: "These are precautionary measures and making an application does not mean they will be introduced.

"However, we must follow the regulatory process to protect water supplies and the environment if dry conditions persist."

The spokesperson said the company was "doing everything possible to protect water supplies" and had reduced leakage by around 25% over the past two years.

They added that the company was taking action as protecting the River Test remains one of its "highest priorities".

What activities will the possible ban affect?

Hampshire and the Isle of Wight were amongst seven English regions declared to be in drought conditions, last month.

According to water regulator Ofwat, while hosepipe bans mainly stop households from using a hose to water their garden, fill a paddling pool or wash their car, NEUBs specifically target businesses.

If the ban comes into force, the activities businesses must stop using water for would include filling or maintaining a non-domestic swimming pool, paddling pool or pond, operating a mechanical vehicle washer and cleaning any vehicle or non-domestic premises.

articles.title: Teams working to avoid 'impactful' wildfires in South West
articles.summary: Rangers and marshals are working to educate people about fire risks on Dartmoor after a dry summer.
articles.body:
People have been urged to avoid starting fires in national parks and moorland due to the dry conditions.

Marshals at Dartmoor National Park in Devon have been on patrol advising people about the risks while firebreaks have also been built to help stop flames spreading.

Deputy head ranger Ella Briens said fires were not allowed in the park as wildfires at this time of year could have a big impact on the surroundings.

Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service said people should not to use disposable barbecues while bonfires, campfires and fireworks should all be avoided.

Briens said the team on Dartmoor had to move people in tents in areas closed to camping and found the remains of barbecues which had scorched the parched grass around them.

She added other fire hazards include discarded bottles.

"We just don't want glass lying around, it's going to be a source of ignition if the sun shines through that," Briens said.

In May 2025, a large wildfire on Dartmoor destroyed about 1,230 acres (5 sq km) of land.

Ranger Luke Engel, speaking to the BBC after spotting another discarded barbecue and abandoned tent at Cadover Bridge, said: "All it takes sometimes is a bit of wood, a spark just spreading to another bit, and when the ground's really dry it can spread anywhere."

Dartmoor fire marshal Lewis Edwards said people sometimes needed "a gentle nudge in the right direction" to make sure they are being safe and using the right areas for camping.

He said because of the heatwaves, marshals had to "step in and really clamp down on people having open fires, disposable barbecues and things like that".

Visitors were more aware of the risk, he said, with the extra signage on the moor and the alert sent by the government to mobile phones.

"We just need to keep promoting it," he added.

The Dartmoor team's warnings came after Devon's assistant chief fire officer Darren Mclatchey said most wildfire incidents were directly impacted by humans from "careless disposal, accidental and deliberate fires".

Fire service officials in Devon and Cornwall said crews had dealt with hundreds of fires in the open during the summer.

Mclatchey said the government's temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues "does help" and added they "aren't necessarily a dangerous item" if they were disposed of "carefully and considerately".

He said the service was planning for the pressures of coping with climate change.

"We absolutely recognise that there's a long-term if not permanent change in climate," he said.

"Part of our planning and preparation is to look at how we will respond to wide-scale incidents, how we prepare for it and how we invest into it."

Mclatchey added: "We have the resources that we need, we will plan for the future as best as possible.

"But I think ultimately it's going to be very difficult for anybody to plan to know exactly what the future will hold we just have to respond to it and plan to it as best we can."

He said they were looking at the risks and "invest into the right area so we're able to respond appropriately".

The service was planning its response to El Niño which could bring powerful winds and "what that might look at for our region".

Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service said crews had received a "high volume" of 999 calls since Friday and would be unable to attend reports of neighbours using barbecues, fire pits or bonfires in private gardens unless there was an immediate threat to life, property or the environment.

Firefighters said it would discourage people from doing open burning as the conditions meant even small fires could "spread rapidly and become difficult to control".

"With Cornwall currently in official drought conditions and a hosepipe ban in force, Cornwall Fire Service is also urging residents, landowners and visitors to avoid carrying out any controlled burns," a fire service spokesperson said.

"Ground and vegetation conditions across the county remain exceptionally dry, significantly increasing the likelihood of fire spread.

"Without immediate and effective means of extinguishment, a controlled burn can quickly escalate, endangering people, property, wildlife and the natural environment."

articles.title: How will extreme weather in the West affect our food?
articles.summary: The impact of recent extreme heat is affecting farmers and putting pressure on our food system.
articles.body:
It has been a difficult year for farmers in the West of England as a result of the five heatwaves that have gripped the UK, scorching fields, plummeting crop yields, and leaving us in drought.

Climate scientists say extreme weather is becoming more likely , posing greater challenges to food production from farm to fork.

With a large farming industry in the region, what does this mean for the food on our plates?

"I think the consumers are going to notice that it's going to cost more money for their food," says farmer Tom Collins from Malmesbury, Wiltshire.

'Warrior' baby home after 304 days in hospital

Meningitis survivor feels 'unstoppable' on UK run

'My footballer brother hid his sexuality for years'

"There's going to be less parsnips, less carrots, less potatoes.

"All the vegetables that grow in the ground have just not had any moisture or rain on them."

It has been an "incredibly tough" summer for Collins, who has been farming for 25 years.

"I've never known a summer like it. Relentless heat every day is just exhausting," he says.

His staff have had to endure long days working in 30C heat, and the prolonged heat and dry weather have caused his spring beans to fail.

"We're probably £30,000 down on our bean income, and we've had to endure the same cost," he says.

Andrew Opie, director of food & sustainability policy at the British Retail Consortium, says extreme weather can affect crop yields and place upward pressure on prices.

"Retailers are experienced in managing supply disruptions and will take all necessary steps, including sourcing from alternative suppliers where appropriate, to minimise any impact on customers," he says.

Pete Falloon, Professor of climate resilient food systems at the University of Bristol, says the biggest challenge for food systems is likely to be the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events.

He says gradual climate changes can often be adapted to over time through changes in crop varieties or farming practices, but sudden extremes are much harder to manage.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) previously warned there could be a shortage of certain food products if drought conditions continue.

Some foods are more vulnerable than others, such as fresh fruit and vegetables, which have shorter growing cycles.

But staple crops like wheat are traded globally and benefit from storage buffers.

However, the UK imports a significant amount of food from overseas, meaning food prices and availability may be influenced by climate impacts overseas.

"Many of the places we get things like apples, oranges, berries, other vegetable crops, peppers, lettuce, in the wider Mediterranean area are also set to see significant increases in water shortages and high temperature extremes in a changing climate," says Falloon.

"The biggest impacts of things like food prices and food availability due to changing climate are likely to be on low-income groups, those living in poverty and the more vulnerable folks in society."

The UK has already experienced significant impacts from extreme weather in recent years.

This saw record-breaking temperatures, reaching up to 36.7C (98F) in Merryfield, Somerset.

According to Climate Change Committee assessments from 2025, climate-related impacts on agriculture are already costing up to billions of pounds annually.

The impacts of extreme heat extend through the food supply chain, causing stress to outdoor workers, straining refrigerating systems, changing consumer preferences and increasing food safety risks from improper storage.

Livestock suffer significantly during extreme heat, experiencing reduced productivity, health issues, and mortality.

Falloon recalls the effects of the 2022 heatwave, which led to several million premature deaths of housed poultry and increased deaths during livestock transport.

"Chicken meat production was lower partly because of animal heat stress, about 9% lower than the sort of recent average," he says.

It is projected that the UK will see hotter, drier summers and warmer, wetter winters.

But wet winters can be just as damaging as droughts.

The exceptionally wet conditions in 2024 caused difficult planting conditions for wheat , problems harvesting crops and reduced access to fields for machinery.

Falloon says these impacts can create a greater variability in food supply and potentially reduce the nutritional quality of some crops.

However, farming adaptation can help manage the impacts of extreme weather.

Debbie Wilkins, who runs Norton Court Farm, says she is learning to adapt to the changing climate.

Growing up as a child on the family-owned farm, she remembers it flooding once every five to six years.

Rather than planting arable crops on fields vulnerable to flooding, she has converted them to types of grass that are more resilient to flooding.

To mitigate the heat, she has planted more trees and hedges.

"I've always tried to be a nature-friendly mixed farm. That's helped us to be more resilient," she says.

"The type of farming I'm operating is a low-input farming, it produces less outputs but is more resilient."

Falloon says there are many practical adaptation measures already available that a growing number of farmers are engaging with.

These include planting crops earlier, using more climate-resilient varieties, improving irrigation efficiency, increasing soil organic matter, and growing deeper-rooting grasses.

"There are lots of reasons to be optimistic if we can use the information we have about future climate change, its impacts on food and farming, and work with farmers and the wider food system to understand what effective ways of building resilience might look like going forward," he says.

articles.title: Mum wants people to know 'there is hope after pregnancy loss'
articles.summary: Hayley Metcalfe, 37, suffered the loss of two babies at 17 and 19 weeks into the pregnancies.
articles.body:
A woman who welcomed a daughter after two pregnancy losses has said she wants others who face similar heartache to know "there is still hope".

Hayley Metcalfe, 37, from Runcorn in Cheshire, said she and her husband Mike were "over the moon" to find out she was pregnant with her second son in 2023.

But what followed was three years of heartbreak when Hayley suffered a placental abruption at 19 weeks pregnant and was told her baby boy, who they had named Oscar, had died.

The following year, the couple lost a second baby, who they had named Leo, at 17 weeks pregnant.

"The road after baby loss is never easy and trusting again can feel impossible," said Hayley.

"But I want people to know there can still be hope."

Hayley said the couple had always wanted to start a family and, in 2019, the pair welcomed their eldest son George.

She recalled how she had a normal pregnancy with George so when she fell pregnant again in 2023, her and husband Mike were excited to grow their family.

But at 19 weeks and four days into her pregnancy, Hayley said she felt as though "something wasn't right".

An ultrasound later confirmed that Oscar had died.

"It sounds awful, but when you know your baby is no longer alive, you just want it all to be over," she said.

"We already had so many baby things at home.

"We told George that his little brother wasn't going to be coming home."

Hayley was induced into labour the following day.

"I was in labour for nine hours and it was incredibly difficult knowing I would never hear my baby cry," she recalled.

"After the funeral, the support from other people gradually faded and life simply carried on, even though I was consumed by grief."

A post-mortem examination later revealed Hayley had suffered a silent, concealed placental abruption, meaning her placenta had separated from the wall of the womb.

In summer 2024, Hayley said she was "terrified" when she became pregnant again.

"We didn't want to feel like we were replacing Oscar, but part of us still hoped we'd be able to have another straightforward pregnancy like we had with George," she said.

"We were delighted - but naturally terrified."

But at 17 weeks, Hayley was told she had lost the pregnancy after suffering a placental abruption.

"I was still grieving Oscar and now our baby boy Leo was gone too," she said.

After three years of loss, Hayley said she began to desperately search for answers and found Tommy's Rainbow Clinic in Manchester - a specialist service for women and their families in a pregnancy following a stillbirth or neonatal death.

It was here that when Hayley fell pregnant in 2025, she was told there was a problem with blood flow from her placenta to the baby.

From six weeks, she started taking daily blood-thinning injections and aspirin.

"I was terrified throughout the pregnancy," she said.

"Every single day I thought the baby was going to die.

"The further along I got, the more I felt there was to lose, because I already knew exactly what losing a baby felt like."

But in February, the couple welcomed their daughter into the world.

"Hope, let out her first cry and I burst into tears," she said. "Everything was finally going to be okay.

"Naming our miracle daughter Hope felt right after everything we'd been through to bring her safely into the world.

"We will always carry the grief of losing Oscar and Leo with us, but Hope is living proof that even after the darkest of storms, rainbows can break through."

articles.title: Northern Ireland artist and business backlash against AI slop
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence becomes part of our everyday lives, there are some railing against cheaply produced material they say is empty and puts real artists' jobs at risk.
articles.body:
When they first started appearing, it was hard to tell where they were coming from, these posters, flyers and food menus that all looked like they had rolled off the same industrial printing press.

Belfast was awash with them during Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann this month, but by that time most people had them sussed out.

"More AI," they sighed, glancing at a caricatured guitarist on a gig poster or an abnormally glistening burger on a menu.

There were even several images of Ed Sheeran appearing to be making his way around the city.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become part of our everyday lives, and has proven useful for businesses who want to produce promotional material quickly and at little-to-no cost.

But there is a growing backlash from creatives and venue owners, who say 'AI slop' is artistically empty and putting real artists' jobs at risk.

The American Bar in Belfast became one of the first businesses in Northern Ireland to declare itself an AI-free zone, and other bars and restaurants have since ridden in behind.

And the backlash is happening in other places too .

Chris Ferry, who makes greeting cards that specialise in the famous Londonderry sense of humour, doesn't think there is much to joke about when it comes to AI.

In a recent video that attracted thousands of engagements online, he warned customers not to "be coming to me asking me to print a birthday card you've made on ChatGPT ever again".

"It's an insult to me, it's an insult to everybody in the creative industry, and it's an insult to the hard work I've put in here," he said.

Artists of all kinds have reported feeling threatened and cheated by AI.

But Ferry thinks the public don't appreciate that AI-generated imagery risks making graphic designers redundant "the same way AI music disadvantages musicians".

"It's exactly the same but people don't seem to get it," he said.

Recently people have visited his shop and asked him to print designs they created using AI, which he said demonstrates a dissonance around how AI is impacting graphic designers like him.

"I'm very proud and passionate about what I do. I'm a designer, not a print shop, so you come in with a scenario and I'll turn it into a design, and that's why our business works, because we're very different."

Ferry said these instances "really annoyed" him but that he didn't blame the customers.

"It's everywhere, it's convenient, and people just aren't thinking of the repercussions for people like me, so I don't hold it against them.

"The customers who brought in the AI stuff offered to pay but I declined and explained why. It's the principle."

He is "worried about the potential long-term consequences" AI might have on business but he said hopes "the very specific nature of the Derry sense of humour" and "the fact people want stuff made by real people" will future-proof Ferry Clever.

Frances Smyth is a freelance graphic designer who said AI is weighing heavy on her mind too.

When she graduated in 2021 "AI wasn't very present" in her degree.

Now a part-time lecturer at Ulster University and somebody whose job has been affected by the pivot to AI within the creative industry, Smyth said she contemplates the rapidly growing technology a lot.

"Students aren't necessarily encouraged to use it but everybody who is creative has to think about it, because it's so prominent in our industries now."

Many creative agencies, she said, are haemorrhaging clients, as businesses turn to AI for reduce marketing costs.

"As soon as savings is mentioned now, one of the first things businesses think is, 'Could we can use ChatGPT to do that?'

"Often the answer is, 'Yeah, sure'. But the problem is that ChatGPT doesn't do as good a job as an actual artist would. It can't replicate like that authentic artistic expression."

She said AI can be "used for a quick turnaround" but is "regurgitative and soulless".

"Even bad art is better than AI slop. I'd much rather see like a gig poster or a menu done on a post-it note than I would to see it put into ChatGPT.

"Like, I honestly would. It has so much more integrity."

Some venues have recently taken "a principled stance" against the use of AI on their premises, including Mandela Hall, located inside Queen's University Student's Union.

This month, the American Bar in Belfast said it "made the decision to boycott the use of AI" in the pub and on social media.

This included all AI-made artistic material, from music to gig posters.

They said "it constitutes a very real threat to the livelihood of artists" and that the "detriment that AI use has on the environment is well documented".

Speaking to BBC NI, co-owner Tomas Gorman said he believed AI is "a deeply damaging technology, particularly for our local artists and those working in the creative industries".

Co-owner Peter McCloskey added: that "even a shoddily made poster cobbled together by the most inexperienced and computer shy of designers holds within it infinitely more creative value and interesting perspective" than AI.

Like many businesses during the Fleadh, Mal Houston from Three Rivers Restaurant used AI posters to highlight entertainment offerings and food deals.

Then somebody put a sticker on a few of his flyers, reading: "Say no to AI."

"I don't know who had time to do that during the fleadh, but it did make me think."

Houston recently announced that his restaurant and nightclub would no longer be using AI-generated art, "even if it does save a few shillings".

"Hospitality is going through a tough time at the minute, so AI can be convenient and cheap if you need a flyer or menu made up.

"But the other side of that is that it is putting graphic designers out of jobs.

"And just like the hospitality industry is struggling because of challenges we're facing, they're struggling because of AI.

"And that's not fair. These are creative people who've paid to develop their talents at university and because of AI the work just isn't there."

So, while AI remains in its ascendancy and continues to proliferate, a small local - and global - backlash has begun.

And Frances Smyth believes the fight against it is there to be won or lost by each individual.

"People have a sense that the march of AI is inexorable, like we need to embrace it and like it's going to happen anyway.

"But it's not inevitable. Like just I've disabled as much as possible on all my devices and I'm saying no.

"You can do that - say no. We don't need that slop in our lives."

articles.title: Planes, helicopters, crews: How Europe is scrambling to contain a record wildfire season
articles.summary: Europe News: Wildfires are stretching firefighting capacity across Europe, forcing countries to move aircraft, helicopters and crews across borders as several blaz.
articles.body: Wildfires are stretching firefighting capacity across Europe, forcing countries to move aircraft, helicopters and crews across borders as several blazes burn at the same time. Serbia is using both Russian and EU assistance, while crews in Ankara brought a large wooded-area fire under control early Monday after an eight-hour operation.By August 19, fires had burned 619,298 hectares across the EU, more than twice the 2006-2025 average of 280,045 hectares for the same point in the year, according to the EU's Joint Research Centre. The European Commission has described this summer's operation as the bloc's largest-ever wildfire response, with 777 firefighters from 14 countries pre-positioned in high-risk areas alongside 22 firefighting planes and five helicopters.Serbia adds EU support after Russian deploymentSerbian authorities said on Sunday that the fire at Deliblatska Pescara, a protected nature reserve where blazes had burned for weeks, had been localised and extinguished, with crews continuing to guard against flare-ups. The fire on Mt Stolovi near Kraljevo was reported under control by Sunday, after inaccessible terrain had complicated firefighting operations.Serbia had initially sought Moscow's help after its interior ministry said no firefighting aircraft "of this capacity" was available through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. A Russian Emergencies Ministry IL-76P firefighting aircraft arrived in Nis on August 19 and began operating over Deliblatska Pescara the next day.At that point, Serbia had not activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, although the bloc said it was ready to provide assistance suited to conditions on the ground. Belgrade subsequently activated the mechanism, bringing EU aircraft and ground crews into an operation that already included Russian support.The EU sent four rescEU Black Hawk helicopters to Serbia â two from the Czech Republic and one each from Slovakia and Romania. A 69-member Romanian firefighting and rescue team with 15 vehicles also joined the response, while teams from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic were involved in firefighting operations by Sunday.Earlier in the summer, Serbia had contributed to Europe's cross-border response by sending a firefighting helicopter and emergency personnel to help tackle fires in Spain through the same EU mechanism. It later sought international assistance as fires spread at home.Bulgaria clears Russian plane under humanitarian exceptionThe Russian deployment required special clearance because EU sanctions imposed after Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine generally bar Russian aircraft from the bloc's airspace. Bulgaria, an EU and Nato member, authorised the IL-76P to cross its airspace under a humanitarian firefighting exception after Belgrade requested permission, according to Bulgaria's transport ministry.The European Commission told Reuters that there could be no "business as usual" with Moscow while Russia continued its war in Ukraine. Serbia continues to seek EU membership but has not joined sanctions imposed on Russia over the war, while maintaining longstanding ties with Moscow.Ankara blaze contained after eight-hour operationThe fire in Ankara broke out on Sunday evening in a wooded area of Mamak on the eastern outskirts of the Turkish capital and spread across a large area. Firefighters brought it under control after about eight hours early Monday, while cooling operations continued to prevent fresh flare-ups, according to Anadolu Agency.Ankara mayor Mansur Yavas said 47 vehicles and 148 personnel were deployed, supported by 20 municipal tankers and four pieces of heavy machinery. The Ankara governor's office said authorities had detained a person they identified as responsible for starting the fire, while an investigation into the circumstances of the blaze continued.The Ankara fire comes amid a wider series of investigations into forest fires across Turkey. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal proceedings had been opened over 73 forest fires in 25 provinces since June 1, with authorities identifying 46 suspects, arresting 12 and placing 21 under judicial supervision.Although the Deliblatska Pescara fire had been extinguished and the Ankara blaze contained, crews continued monitoring affected areas for flare-ups as firefighting resources remained deployed across the region. The overlapping emergencies have kept aircraft, helicopters and personnel moving across borders as authorities remain alert for fresh outbreaks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A landslide at a landfill in the capital of Guinea kills 30 people, officials say
articles.summary: A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea‘s capital of Conakry early on Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government.
articles.body: A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea‘s capital of Conakry early on Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government. Authorities said that heavy rains, which started at around 2 a.m., washed over the refuse at Dar Es Salam — the largest landfill in Conakry — and triggered a landslide that buried nearby shacks. A search and rescue operation was underway to find survivors. Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed. The site, an open-air waste dump which is the largest in the city, had been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion. Locals living around the landfill had been given eviction notices, which forced many to leave the area, but many others were still around at the time of the disaster, according to authorities. “We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere,” Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene. Guinea is mineral-rich with huge deposits of bauxite — the largest in the world — and also has iron ore, gold, diamonds and minerals. However, according to the World Bank, 43.7% of the population lives below the national poverty line.

articles.title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
articles.summary: Using the carcinogen to preserve food is prohibited in China, the world's largest producer of cabbages.
articles.body:
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.

Officials in the north-eastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.

An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical used for preserving biological specimens that is known to cause cancer, for keeping food fresh is strictly prohibited in China.

China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.

Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.

Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.

Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.

Local authorities in Kangbao county said in a statement issued on Saturday: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."

Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.

The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.

An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."

China produces well over 30 million tonnes of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.

Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Trump is trying to tighten the screws on an Iran numb to economic pain
articles.summary: Iran, already drained by years of sanctions and a brutal military onslaught from the United States and Israel, now faces another test as President Donald Trump moves to further tighten the economic screws on the Islamic Republic.
articles.body: Iran, already drained by years of sanctions and a brutal military onslaught from the United States and Israel, now faces another test as President Donald Trump moves to further tighten the economic screws on the Islamic Republic. The US Treasury Department on Monday threatened sweeping new sanctions on countries that refuse to cut economic ties with Iran as part of what it has cast as an “economic D-Day” for the country — though it stopped short of immediately imposing the most severe penalties. In a bid to ramp up pressure on Tehran, the Trump administration said it had expanded the categories of “Iran-related conduct” that could trigger future sanctions, including activity in sectors such as digital assets, technology and shipping that Washington says help sustain Iran’s economy. The administration said it also plans to work with counterparts around the world to curb activity linked to Tehran and would give countries defined timelines to wind down ties with the country. The measures come as the Trump administration seeks to increase pressure on Tehran amid deadlocked talks to end the six-month war and as Iran continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy supplies. By the admission of its own top officials, Iranians are already suffering a host of economic problems. “We are apologetic that these problems exist, as we find ourselves in a full-scale economic, military, and security war,” Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said before the new Treasury measures were announced, according to state media. “As the government, we are seeking with all our being to steer inflation, public problems, people’s livelihoods, people’s jobs, people’s future, and people’s lives towards dignity and pride,” he added. Videos on social media published last week showed empty markets in Tehran and Karaj, with sellers complaining that their fresh produce is not being bought. One resident of Tehran and another business owner told CNN that economic pressures have become “untenable.” Not only is everything expensive, Nima, a 36-year-old resident of Tehran, told CNN, but some of the “important things needed we can’t even get, like certain medications.” An owner of a small shop who chose to remain anonymous to speak freely about the economic conditions said he is barely making ends meet. “We are running out of some of the foreign products like foreign shampoo and conditioner, toothpaste. We have limited stock and it’s now too expensive for most people, but even the Iranian-made products I’ve had to raise prices on,” he said. ‘Immediate pain’ But even with fresh economic pressure, experts say that unless the Trump administration uncovers fresh methods to choke off Tehran’s revenue streams, Washington will once again face a regime long practiced in sanction evasion, resourceful at finding new ways to generate income, and betting on its ability to survive the US’ economic pressure. Over decades of international pariahdom, the Islamic Republic was forced to develop sophisticated methods to mitigate the impact of Western sanctions, creating a decentralized network of front companies, brokers, exchange houses, and a shadow tanker fleet that uses ship-to-ship transfers, altered tracking data, and false documentation to move oil. In 2024, $9 billion of Iranian shadow banking activity occurred through US correspondent accounts, the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said, based on reporting from American financial institutions. Shell companies, including those in oil, shipping, and investment, facilitate billions of dollars in transactions through networks spanning the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, and Singapore, according to the Treasury Department. Payments are often made in the Chinese yuan, through barter arrangements, or outside the dollar-based banking system, Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University told CNN. The latest measures will “squash” the economy of “this murderous regime” and curtail Iran’s ability to “project power through their proxies” and its ability to pay the Iranian military, Bessent told CNBC in a recent interview. But experts said that ordinary Iranians will most likely bear the brunt of the new sanctions. “Ordinary Iranians will experience the most immediate pain, and further sanctions would weaken the rial, increase inflation, raise the cost of imported goods and industrial inputs, and reduce household purchasing power,” Shokri said. Even if public and military spending, as well as regional allies, suffer under the new strict economic sanctions, it will be the wage earners, pensioners, small businesses, and lower-income families that would be particularly vulnerable, he added. The “politically connected” institutions and intermediaries would be partially “insulated” as they continue profiting from smuggling, currency manipulation, and control over scarce imports, Shokri said. Experts say that for the US to effectively target Iran’s economy, it will need to target major Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, independent refineries, and banks processing Iranian revenue, but that could also risk retaliation from Beijing against Washington. In a Truth Social post Trump threatened other countries with “tremendous economic consequences” if they provide any type of “lifeline” to Iran, without naming specific nations. Washington would have to target the central nodes of Iran’s trade rather than continue sanctioning replaceable vessels and shell companies,” Shokri said, adding that the US could aim to sanction tanker managers, insurers, ports, ship-to-ship transfer providers while adding more restrictions on technology that could end up with dual-use military functions. ‘Weather The Storm’ Even though the Iranian government has expanded domestic production while operating its sophisticated network of front companies to procure essential goods, largely from China, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated that it can transfer the sanctions burden onto an already struggling population while protecting the institutions essential for the regime’s survival. Weeks before the war, Iranians took to the streets to protest rising costs and inflation. Yet after initially acknowledging the economic struggle, the government once again accused the protesters of being foreign agents before unleashing one of the worst crackdowns in the Islamic Republic’s history. For now, the Iranian regime is using the war to justify poor economic conditions and a once struggling government has been given an excuse to its exhausted population, while it is arguably Trump who faces greater political pressure from US consumers angry at gas prices ahead of midterms. “They are willing to weather the storm, and they are willing to go through the pain,” Dina Esfandiary, Middle East geoeconomics lead at Bloomberg Economics told CNN. “None of the measures that President Trump is contemplating are going to make Iran capitulate.” What is required, Esfandiary says, is “diplomacy and carrots” with Iran, which “of course is not at all being contemplated.” For now, Neda, a 34-year-old Tehran resident struggling with kidney disease and needing medication, is holding her breath as she is once again forced to buy only half of her monthly dose. “I have so much anxiety all the time because without the medication I won’t really survive,” she said. “You know, I went to the doctor the other day and the nurse said people weren’t even able to show up to their appointments for dialysis.” “The people receiving chemotherapy stopped going because they just cannot afford it anymore.”

articles.title: Liberia once offered Black Americans a new home. Decades on, it is receiving migrants the US wants out
articles.summary: Is Liberia an American dumping ground — or a place where a new generation of arrivals can build a new life?
articles.body: Is Liberia an American dumping ground — or a place where a new generation of arrivals can build a new life? That’s the question Liberians are asking themselves after the first people to be deported to the West African country from the United States arrived in the capital, Monrovia. The 20 people on the flight from Louisiana were the first to be sent under an agreement that could see up to 1,200 people transferred to Liberia, a country of less than 6 million people, many of them descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans. Liberian officials said the new arrivals were from “African and western hemisphere countries.” Liberia is one of several countries that have agreed to take migrants being deported from the US under the Trump administration’s anti-immigration crackdown. The arrivals are coming to a nation whose history is deeply tied to migration from the US. Nearly two centuries ago, free and formerly enslaved Black Americans crossed the Atlantic to settle in what would become Liberia – a name that translates as “land of the free.” Now, a country shaped in part by that migration is accepting people the US wants to remove. For Liberians, that has thrown up a mix of feelings in a country still recovering from a long and bloody civil war. “This country is going through a lot, and having more people come in — can we handle all of this?” said Pheta Morris, 48, a descendant of the Black Americans who settled in Liberia. But she said she sees the new arrivals through the lens of Liberia’s history and is struck by the contrast. “I think about the Americo-Liberians — people who were rejected where they were and needed somewhere to go, and Liberia opened its arms to them,” she said. “Back then, people needed somewhere they could be free, accepted and welcomed. Now, people are being rejected from the US, and Liberia is opening its doors to them.” The first transfer has already faced complications. Reuters reported that five migrants who refused to disembark after arriving in Monrovia were flown instead to Equatorial Guinea in Central Africa, where they are held with more than 30 other migrants previously sent there by the US. A US State Department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority,” adding that the department generally does not comment on private diplomatic communications with other governments. CNN has contacted Liberia’s information ministry for more details about the agreement and its terms. A country shaped by America The first group of free Black Americans arrived in Liberia in the early 1820s. Over the following decades, thousands more made the journey, with the American Colonization Society helping to establish settlements along the West African coast. The US State Department says about 16,000 Black Americans migrated to Liberia during the 19th century. The migration was complicated. Some Black Americans saw Liberia as a chance to escape racism and build a new life, while others opposed the colonization movement and rejected the idea that free Black people should leave the US. Africans rescued from slave ships by the US Navy were also brought to Liberia. The settlements eventually formed the Republic of Liberia, which declared independence in 1847. The American influence remains visible today. Liberia’s flag resembles that of the US; its capital was named Monrovia after America’s fifth President James Monroe, and its early institutions were heavily influenced by Washington. Conmany Wesseh, a former Liberian lawmaker and member of the ruling Unity Party who was nominated as Liberia’s ambassador to the United Nations and later the European Union under former president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, said that history continues to shape how Liberians view the US. For Wesseh though, the arrival of the deportees raises a more immediate question: Can Liberia, a country still struggling with basic infrastructure and services, accommodate more people? The cost of taking them in Liberia began rebuilding after a 14-year civil war ended in 2003, but Wesseh said the country still needs major investment. Poverty levels remain high and youth unemployment stands at 40%, according to African Development Bank data. “Our country needs a great deal of support,” he said. “We are short on medical facilities, and we have problems with education.” He questioned how the country would manage an influx of people from abroad. “They will have to go to the same hospitals. You won’t create a new hospital for them,” he said. “There’s no spare housing. We don’t have existing housing to put new people in.” Wesseh said Liberia’s development needs may have influenced the government’s decision, with officials hoping the agreement would bring support from Washington. Liberian authorities described the arrangement as humanitarian and said the deportees will be treated as guests who can seek asylum or leave the country. Asked whether he viewed the deal as humanitarian assistance, a diplomatic arrangement or the US outsourcing its immigration enforcement, Wesseh chose the latter. “I think (the administration of US President Donald Trump) just sees this as a place to dump people,” he said. “They want to take them off their hands and dump them in this country.” A chance for a new start Francis Dennis had long known that his family had roots in the migration of Black Americans to Liberia in the 19th century. But just a few weeks ago, he became curious about his family’s past and began using AI genealogy tools to dig deeper into that history. The 71-year-old former president of the Liberia Chamber of Commerce told CNN he traced his great-great-great-grandfather to Snow Hill, a town on Maryland’s Eastern Shore in the US, using the technology and notes left by his father. He said the research also pointed him to the name of the vessel that carried his ancestor across the Atlantic to Liberia, along with a list of its passengers. Generations later, Dennis is watching another group arrive in Liberia from the US. But he does not believe their circumstances have to define what comes next. “People may have their apprehension about a new life, but it’s also an opportunity,” he said. “Some may be happy, some may resent it, but it opens a new window, a new opportunity.” His own ancestor crossed the Atlantic generations ago and became part of the community that helped shape modern Liberia. Now, he hopes those arriving under very different circumstances will also see the country as a chance for a fresh start. “The ball will be in their court,” Dennis said. “Are they going to seize it as an opportunity for a new start, a fresh start, a new life? Or will they be thinking about the past?”

articles.title: A landslide at a landfill in the capital of Guinea kills 30 people, officials say
articles.summary: A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea ‘s capital of Conakry early Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government.
articles.body: CONAKRY, Guinea — A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea’s capital of Conakry early Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government. Authorities said that heavy rains, which started around 2 a.m., washed over the refuse at Dar Es Salam — the largest landfill in Conakry — and triggered a landslide that buried nearby shacks. A search and rescue operation was underway to find survivors. Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed. The site, an open-air waste dump that is the largest in the city, had been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion. Locals living around the landfill had been given eviction notices, which forced many to leave the area, but many others were still around at the time of the disaster, according to authorities. “We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere,” Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene. Guinea is mineral-rich with huge deposits of bauxite — the largest in the world — and also has iron ore, gold, diamonds and minerals. However, according to the World Bank, 43.7% of the population lives below the national poverty line.

articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the âcontinued failureâ of authorit.
articles.body: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the âcontinued failureâ of authorities at a state-run hospital, alleging that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications.In a statement on Sunday, PTI central secretary Information Sheikh Waqas Akram said authorities had failed to provide the 73-year-old Khan with the medically recommended diagnostic test despite a functional CT scanner being available at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Dawn reported."This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,â Akram said.Akram also cited a Supreme Court order directing Khan to undergo a comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International Hospital.He alleged that authorities had bypassed the directive and instead transferred Khan to a facility where the CT angiography was not conducted.âWhen the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Khan to a hospital unable or unwilling to perform the procedure raises a grave question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CT Coronary Angiography from being conducted?â he asked."Even the governmentâs own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,â Akram added.Akram said a government medical board examined Khan on August 10 after he complained of heart palpitations and severe headaches.He said a cardiologist at PIMS had recommended a CTA on August 1 after Khan experienced fluctuating blood pressure and restlessness, citing potential cardiac complications given his age and prolonged isolation.Taking note of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary, to establish the facts and determine responsibility.Commenting on the Prime Ministerâs decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports that Imran Khanâs CTA was not conducted, Akram said the move raised âserious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities thereâ."Imran Khanâs heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,â Akram said."Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,â he alleged."The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,â Akram added.Meanwhile, former India captains Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar are among 21 former international cricket captains who have written to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging authorities to ensure proper medical treatment and the welfare of Imran Khan.The letter, initiated by former Australia captain Greg Chappell, marks the second appeal by former international cricketers calling for humane treatment and adequate medical care for the 73-year-old Khan.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023, in connection with a corruption case and has remained in custody since then. articles.title: EU, Russian aircraft help Serbia battle wildfires
articles.summary: EU and Russian aircraft help Serbia fight major wildfires as extreme heat fuels fires across the Balkans.
articles.body:
Russian and European Union aircraft have been helping Serbian teams battle wildfires burning across the country, including a blaze that has raged for weeks in a protected nature reserve near the capital, Belgrade, according to state media.

The operation in Deliblatska Pescara continued into Monday, as Serbia’s RTS reported that efforts were also underway to extinguish a separate fire in the southwestern Stolovi mountain range.
