Serbia’s Interior Minister, Ivica Dacic, described the situation in Deliblatska Pescara as “extremely difficult,” according to Euro News, with more than 400 personnel deployed to the area each day.

President Aleksandar Vucic said Belgrade had turned to both the EU and Russia once it became clear Serbia’s own resources were not enough.

“The very second we realised that our own forces were no longer sufficient, we immediately requested urgent assistance from Russia and the European mechanism,” he said.

Russia deployed an Ilyushin Il-76 water-bombing aircraft to Serbia on Wednesday, and according to RTS, it had dropped 168 tonnes of water on the two fires on Sunday — 126 tonnes in Deliblatska Pescara and 42 tonnes in Stolovi.

The EU response includes four Black Hawk helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, along with teams of firefighters and vehicles from Germany and Romania.

Serbia is not an EU member but can request aid under the bloc’s Civil Protection Mechanism, a system that allows EU countries to pool emergency resources for disasters. Belgrade formally asked for help on Friday.

Earlier in the summer there, Serbia sent a firefighting helicopter and response team to Spain, when various blazes stretched the bloc’s own resources thin.

Fires are also burning across the border in North Macedonia , where a blaze near the town of Strumica reportedly damaged at least one home.

A large fire meanwhile broke out over the weekend between Bosnia and Croatia, forcing the closure of the main road linking the Bosnian city of Trebinje to the Croatian tourist city of Dubrovnik, stranding thousands of travellers and prompting the evacuation of nearby villages.

The wildfire season now unfolding across the Balkans has been driven by an unusually hot, dry summer that has left much of the region primed to burn.

articles.title: How much more are you spending on petrol since the war on Iran began?
articles.summary: At least 145 countries have reported increases in petrol prices since the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel began.
articles.body:
Since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran six months ago, petrol prices have risen in at least 145 countries, adding to the burden on consumers worldwide.

The figures are based on data from GlobalPetrolPrices, which tracks fuel prices in 170 countries and territories. Petrol prices in Myanmar rose the most, increasing by 56 percent from $0.77 per litre of 95-octane fuel on February 23 to $1.20 on August 17. Bhutan recorded the next-largest increase at 55 percent, followed by Cuba at 51 percent, the UAE at 50 percent and 48 percent in Nigeria.

In 25 other countries, most of them oil producers with heavily subsidised fuel, prices have either remained unchanged or fallen by single digits.

The table below lists the 145 countries where petrol prices at the pump increased over the past six months.

How higher fuel costs shrink your driving range

Before the war, the US national average for a gallon [3.78 litres] of regular petrol was $2.94. It now costs $4.09, an increase of 39 percent, according to AAA Fuel Prices, which tracks retail fuel prices for the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The extra cost directly affects how far people can travel. Before the war, $50 worth of fuel in the US could take a family sedan roughly 718 km (446 miles). Today, the same amount takes you about 536 km (333 miles) – 183 km less, a 25 percent reduction in driving distance.

That gap varies depending on where you live.

Set your country, car and budget below to see how far your money takes you. If you’re filling up in the US, you can also select a state and fuel grade.

How high oil costs drive up the price of food

Oil prices and food prices move in lockstep, with energy prices affecting every stage of the food supply chain, from the fertilisers used in the fields to the trucks that carry food from field to supermarket shelf.

Rising oil prices also directly impact shipping and the cost of transport.

“The lifeblood of the global economy is transport,” economist David McWilliams told Al Jazeera. “It’s getting stuff from A to B – it’s a logistics problem, a supply chain problem and ultimately transportation is the energy of the global economy.”

In lower-income countries, where populations spend a far greater share of their earnings on food and import large quantities of grain and fertiliser, rising oil prices could rapidly translate into food shortages.

What products are made from oil and gas?

Oil and gas are used for far more than just fuel. They are raw materials for thousands of everyday products.

Plastics, including water bottles, food packaging, phone casings and medical syringes, are all derived from crude oil.

Crude oil is also the hidden ingredient in synthetic fabrics, such as polyester, nylon and acrylic, which are used to make everything from sportswear to carpets. It also underpins the cosmetics industry, as it is used to make products such as petroleum jelly (Vaseline), lipsticks and concealers.

Household items also rely on oil-based ingredients, with laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids and paints all derived from petroleum products.

The global food supply is essentially built on natural gas in the form of fertilisers, used to enhance crop yields and ensure that food production can meet demand.

articles.title: Britain’s giving Ukraine access to secret missile technology. Will it make a difference?
articles.summary: Britain will allow the release of classified technology so that a British/French-designed cruise missile can be manufactured in Ukraine, a boost for Kyiv in its efforts to bring more firepower to bear hundreds of kilometers into Russia.
articles.body: Britain will allow the release of classified technology so that a British/French-designed cruise missile can be manufactured in Ukraine, a boost for Kyiv in its efforts to bring more firepower to bear hundreds of kilometers into Russia. Paris and Kyiv want to set up a Ukrainian production line for the SCALP air-launched cruise missile, known as the Storm Shadow in the United Kingdom, by the end of the year. The declassification of information on British-made components of the missiles, announced Monday, is a key step towards that goal. Made by European arms manufacturer MBDA, SCALP is a conventionally armed, long-range, deep-strike weapon, of which Ukraine has used imported versions with success against hardened targets, including in November 2024, when they were fired at targets inside Russia for the first time. Powered by a turbojet engine, it has a maximum range of 550 kilometers (342 miles) and can carry a 400-kilogram (880 pounds) high-explosive penetrating warhead, according to the Missile Threat project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) Once launched, the missile uses a combination of internal, global positioning and terrain reference navigation coupled with “infrared seeker and automatic target recognition algorithms” to achieve a high degree of accuracy in all weather conditions, according to the CSIS. The SCALP is fired from Ukraine’s Su-24 or Mirage 2000 fighter jets and attempts to avoid air defenses by hugging the terrain during flight. Its use for Ukraine will be in striking buried military targets, like command bunkers, something more challenging for the lighter weight drones Kyiv has been using to hit more exposed targets like oil refineries or warehouses. The Kremlin reacted angrily to the announcement, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the UK was “participating in the war” and “pouring fuel on the fire.” His statement came after the Russian embassy in London warned the UK last week that “the deeper its involvement” and “the greater its support” for Ukraine, the “higher the price it will pay.” Britain and France have not announced how many SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles have been supplied to Ukraine to date, but in 2025 manufacturer MBDA reactivated production lines that had been shuttered for 15 years. “Supplied to Ukraine, the Franco-British SCALP/Storm Shadow missile has demonstrated its effectiveness in modern high-intensity combat, in decisive situations,” French Defense Minister Sébastien Lecornu said at the time. Even with the UK announcement, it could take several years for production to scale up, but British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says London is backing Kyiv for the long haul. “The Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes,” Burnham said in a press release Monday announcing that the UK would release its missile technology. “Ukraine’s security is our security,” said the prime minister, who arrived in Kyiv on Monday for Ukraine’s independence day, in his first overseas trip since taking office on July 20. Zelensky said he was “grateful” to Burnham for his support, saying that he awarded Burnham with the “first new state distinction: Gratitude of the Ukrainian People.” The two countries signed an agreement to “develop their partnership in the field of artificial intelligence,” Zelensky said. While in Ukraine, Burnham co-chaired a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a 34-nation international alliance formed last year by Britain and France to support Ukraine in the war as US aid waned under the Trump administration. The alliance promised to boost Ukraine’s air defenses on Monday, with Burnham saying Monday that Kyiv’s allies need to do “everything we can” to supply more air defenses. French President Emmanuel Macron, who joined the meeting remotely, said that the last few weeks have clearly showed that Kyiv’s allies “need to accelerate delivery of interceptors,” adding that his country will accelerate “everything that we have available.” Macron also confirmed that the first full-scale military exercises of the Coalition of the Willing will be conducted in October and November. They will involve British and French forces and take place in Poland. Interceptor struggle What the SCALP can’t address is Ukraine’s shortage of defensive missiles, like the US-designed Patriot system, a vulnerability exposed with devastating consequences in recent weeks as Russia has launched large waves of its own missiles and drones in attacks that have killed dozens of Ukrainians. CNN visited a Patriot battery in Ukraine earlier this month and was told that it had not been fired in weeks because no interceptors were available. Ukraine has asked for permission to manufacture the Patriot interceptors in the country, an idea US President Donald Trump initially supported in early July but later backtracked on. The Trump administration has also rebuffed Ukrainian attempts to acquire long-range US Tomahawk cruise missiles, stocks of which have been taxed by the war in Iran. Ukraine’s domestic missile production has not stood still, however. Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point has developed the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. With a range of 3,000 kilometers, it can strike deep inside Russia, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this month it was used to hit a key Russian rocket electronics facility some 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s border. The Ukrainian leader said the Flamingo made its combat debut in 2025, and open-source intelligence reports indicate its use has been on the increase this year. Fire Point has also developed long-range drones to go along with shorter range ballistic missiles. Kyiv’s use of longer-range weapons has turned Russia’s sprawling land mass, once considered a military advantage, into a problem for Moscow as it struggles to allocate limited defensive weaponry to the increasing number of targets within Ukraine’s range, Peter Dickinson, editor of the Atlantic Council’s Ukraine Alert blog, wrote earlier this month. “A long line of would-be conquerors have invaded Russia only for their armies to swallowed up by the vastness of the country. Ukraine is now attempting to turn this military logic on its head with a strategic bombing campaign that aims to exploit Russia’s immensity and transform it from a key strength into a fatal weakness,” Dickinson wrote.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Plato: "Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins inâ¦"
articles.summary: Europe News: Two people can hit the exact same confusing, unresolved question and respond in completely different ways. One feels the confusion purely as discomfor.
articles.body: Two people can hit the exact same confusing, unresolved question and respond in completely different ways. One feels the confusion purely as discomfort, something to be resolved as quickly as possible by picking whichever answer sounds most reasonable and then moving on without looking back. The other feels that same confusion as something closer to fascination, a genuine puzzle worth sitting inside rather than rushing past on the way to relief. Plato put this second reaction at the very root of philosophical thinking itself. In the dialogue Theaetetus, written around 369 BC, he has Socrates respond to a young mathematician's confusion, his dizziness at realizing he can't fully explain what knowledge actually is, not with reassurance meant to settle the confusion down, but with something closer to approval, telling him that this exact feeling, wonder, is the mark of someone doing philosophy correctly, rather than a sign that something in the conversation has gone wrong. This ancient insight remains remarkably relevant today, reminding us that genuine intellectual growth requires embracing uncertainty rather than rushing toward comfortable, premature conclusions.Quote of the day by Plato: "Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder."Written inside a dialogue about the nature of knowledge itselfWhat gives this line extra weight is the specific conversation it comes from. Theaetetus is structured as an attempt to define knowledge, and across the dialogue, every proposed definition that Theaetetus offers- knowledge as perception, knowledge as true belief, knowledge as true belief with an account- gets carefully taken apart by Socrates, leaving Theaetetus increasingly disoriented rather than increasingly certain. It's at that exact point of disorientation, when the ground seems to be giving way under a concept everyone assumes they already understand, that Socrates names wonder as the beginning of the whole enterprise rather than its failure.That framing reflects something central to how Plato understood philosophy's origins more broadly. His own philosophical life began in the shadow of his teacher Socrates's trial and execution in 399 BC, an event that left Plato deeply unsettled about the relationship between conventional certainty and actual truth, and that pushed him to found the Academy in Athens, widely regarded as one of the first institutions of higher learning in the Western world, built specifically around the same relentless, unsettled questioning that runs through his dialogues. Wonder, for Plato, was never a symptom to be cured on the way to an answer. It was the entry point into philosophy itself, the state a serious thinker was supposed to return to again and again rather than escape as quickly as possible.A simple way to actually use this ideaThe useful move here is treating confusion about something fundamental as a signal worth paying attention to rather than a problem to be resolved as fast as possible. Modern habits often push in the opposite direction, toward quick answers, tidy explanations, and a general discomfort with sitting inside genuine uncertainty for very long. Plato's version of philosophy asks for the opposite instinct: when a familiar concept, knowledge, fairness, happiness, suddenly stops making obvious sense under close examination, that disorientation is not evidence the thinking has gone wrong. It's evidence the thinking has finally reached something worth examining.A fair test, the next time an ordinary assumption suddenly seems less obvious than it did a moment ago, is to ask whether the confusion is worth staying with a little longer rather than being smoothed over immediately. That question won't resolve every genuine puzzle. It usually keeps a real question from being replaced too quickly by a convenient, half-examined answer.Other famous quotes by Plato"The beginning is the most important part of the work." "Ignorance, the root and stem of all evil." "Human behavior flows from three main sources: desire, emotion, and knowledge."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
articles.summary: The Montagu Harrier successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location.
articles.body:
The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported.

A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland.

Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024.

An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year."

Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year.

The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes.

The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed.

The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons.

These slender, long-winged raptors make an epic annual migration to Africa in winter and return to Europe to nest over summer, often setting up home in agricultural fields.

But little is known about the behaviour of juvenile harriers once they leave the nest. This year, for the first time, the RSPB has fitted two of the chicks with satellite tags in the hope of providing the birds with better protection.

"It will allow us for the first time ever to work out where they're going, what migration route, how long they'll spend there, and will they come back to the UK in the first year or the second year," said Mark Thomas, head of investigations at the RSPB.

"All of that information is the bit that's missing from the jigsaw."

It is also hoped the tagging can better protect the rare birds from having their nests, on the ground, hidden among crops, inadvertently destroyed.

"This is a species right on the brink, and climate change is not helping that. The harvest here, for example, this year, was like a month earlier than in previous years. So it almost puts any Montagu's harrier nest at the peril of inadvertently being destroyed by farm machinery," said Thomas.

Conservationists have urged birders to look out for the youngsters, and report any sightings by emailing the RSPB's Montagu's hotline at montys@rspb.org.uk.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V's health has worsened, palace says
articles.summary: Norway's King Harald remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bloodstream bacterial infection.
articles.body:
King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream.

The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice.

The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago.

His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia.

The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026.

Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018.

The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg HÃ¸iby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence.

HÃ¸iby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure.

Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

articles.title: Zolani Tete: Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
articles.summary: One of the suspects is due in court on Monday to be charged with murder and attempted murder.
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.

Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.

One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.

The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.

Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.

The motive behind the attack is unclear.

Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.

According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

articles.title: US firefighters say major blaze near Reno about a quarter contained
articles.summary: But officials fear that winds could fan the flames for two more days, as many locals remain under evacuation orders.
articles.body:
US fire crews have reported progress in their efforts to tackle a large wildfire menacing the city of Reno, Nevada - saying the blaze is about a quarter contained.

The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, had spread over 15,000 acres by Monday, firefighters said.

Evacuation orders remain in place for 23,000 people, though other residents have now been allowed to return to their homes. Tens of thousands of other residents have been told to be ready to leave at any moment.

Officials are concerned that gusts of wind could drive the flames towards more homes. Unfavourable weather conditions are forecast for the next two days, meaning the fire could continue to burn during that timeframe.

No deaths have been reported, though seven people have been injured.

The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, spread in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains near Reno due to those same windy and unpredictable weather conditions.

The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but they do affect large urban areas and part of a highway.

Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants.

In their update on Monday afternoon, fire officials said the blaze had been at least 27% contained.

Chief Richard Edwards, of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said those injured were four civilians and three firefighters, who suffered minor burns.

Edwards added that 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged, and that those numbers were expected to increase. Shelters have been set up in the area to take in displaced residents.

While firefighters have made progress, more than two-thirds of the fire's perimeter remains uncontained.

The fire is thought to have been caused by humans. Edwards added on Monday that investigators did not yet know if the blaze was set intentionally.

Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions more likely that assist the rapid spread of wildfires.

Reno's average temperature has gone up by over 4C since the 1970s, faster than any other big US city, according to Climate Central.

Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo earlier declared a state of emergency in surrounding Washoe County, and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts.

"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said on Saturday.

Firefighters from Australia and New Zealand have so far taken part in the containment effort â as well as crews from 15 US states.

The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city close to the "get set" warning area - previously said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation.

But one student, James Wolfgang Perez, said some teaching staff had independently decided to cancel their classes. The sight of the fire spreading in the direction of the campus on Saturday had been "apocalyptic", he told the BBC.

Justin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and similarly watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles.

He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home.

"We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said.

The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno.

Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people.

Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres.

articles.title: In 1934, an Arizona father began gathering rejected objects and desert Stone; 11 years later, the salvage had become an 18-room castle for his daughter
articles.summary: US News: Discover the story behind Mystery Castle in Arizona, built by Boyce Luther Gulley from discarded materials as a tribute to his daughter Mary Lou. Explore its unique architecture and historical significance.
articles.body: In the foothills of Phoenixâs South Mountain, an extraordinary house was built from materials most people would have thrown away. Between the 1930s and 1945, Boyce Luther Gulley gathered desert stone, rejected bricks, old railway materials, telephone poles, automobile parts and other discarded objects to build an 18-room castle for his daughter, Mary Lou. He worked largely by hand, shaping an eccentric three-level home into the desert landscape without a conventional architectural plan. What began as a private project became one of Phoenixâs most unusual landmarks.Today known as Mystery Castle, the structure stands as a striking example of vernacular architecture and an early exercise in material reuse. The National Trust for Historic Preservation says Gulley built the castle without formal architectural or engineering training, combining local materials, folk-art influences and recycled objects. The building eventually became a nationally recognised attraction, but its story began with a father separated from his young daughter and a promise connected to the sandcastles they had built together.From Seattle to the Arizona desertGulley was a Seattle businessman who had some training in architectural engineering. In the late 1920s, after being diagnosed with tuberculosis, he left his family and travelled to Phoenix, where the dry climate was then considered beneficial for people suffering from the disease. He eventually settled near South Mountain, at a time when the foothills were far less developed than they are today.Mary Lou had enjoyed building sandcastles with her father. The idea of creating something permanent may have stayed with Gulley after he moved west. Over the following years, he began assembling a house from whatever materials he could obtain. The National Trust dated construction of Mystery Castle to about 1934â1945. Architectural historians, however, noted that Gulley had begun building on the site earlier, with the structure evolving gradually rather than following a conventional construction plan. The result was a sprawling house that followed the contours of the hillside rather than imposing a regular architectural grid.A house assembled from what others rejectedThe castleâs unusual appearance was not simply the result of cheap materials. Gulley made the discarded objects part of the building's design. Railroad components became structural or decorative elements, old bricks became architectural details, and stones were carefully arranged into walls, fireplaces, niches and platforms.Historical Archaeology has shown that reusing building materials is not exclusively a modern sustainability idea but has long existed within vernacular building traditions. Inside Mystery Castle, practicality and eccentricity frequently overlap. The 18 rooms include a chapel, a bar and a room known as Purgatory. The building contains 13 fireplaces and a network of stairways and unusual passages. Built-in furniture was incorporated directly into the masonry, while some windows and decorative features were made from salvaged materials.The result was a building in which almost every feature carried a story about its previous life. Materials that might otherwise have been overlooked or discarded were given new functions within the castle, making the structure as much a collection of reused objects as a home. Its unconventional construction also reflected Gulleyâs determination to build according to his own ideas, without following the standard plans or materials used in conventional houses.Mary Lou inherits the castleMary Lou was 22 when she learned that her father had left her the property. She and her mother, Frances, travelled to Arizona and moved into the castle. The castle soon acquired another identity. In 1948, LIFE magazine featured Mary Lou and the unusual house in a story that helped give it the name Mystery Castle. The attention drew curious visitors, and Mary Lou and her mother later began offering tours. For decades, Mary Lou became the property's principal keeper and public guide, sharing the story of the building with visitors.Mary Lou died in 2010 after living at the castle for many decades. Before her death, she established a foundation to help preserve the property. The structure later faced another challenge. After vandalism and break-ins, Mystery Castle closed to the public in 2023, and a subsequent assessment found that stabilisation, repairs and accessibility improvements would cost about $3.3 million.In 2024, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed Mystery Castle on its list of Americaâs 11 Most Endangered Historic Places. The designation brought renewed attention to a building whose greatest strength and weakness are closely connected: it was built as a highly individual, handmade structure rather than a conventional one designed for easy maintenance. Rejected bricks, old metal, desert rock and salvaged household materials were given new purposes and assembled into something that could not have been produced from a standard building plan. What survived was not simply a house, but an intensely personal architectural landscape built piece by piece for a daughter who would spend much of her life caring for it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: E1 settlement: Why Netanyahu, Israel’s right might not mind global outrage
articles.summary: The settlement threatens Palestinian statehood. But it could help Israel’s PM, other far-right leaders before elections.
articles.body:
The Israeli government last week invited bids for the building of more than 1,200 units, a key step towards the construction of the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank just two months before Israel’s general election.

E1 (East 1) would link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two. Both supporters and critics agree that its construction would end the possibility of a Palestinian state.

list 1 of 4 Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence

list 2 of 4 Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan

list 3 of 4 Europe, Canada condemn Israeli plans for new West Bank settlement

list 4 of 4 Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage

The move has drawn international outrage, including from the United Nations.

But sections of Israel’s political class are using this global backlash to their own ends and could frame their support for E1 as a key pitch in their election campaigns.

Many on Israel’s right, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, thrive on the international outrage their comments and plans draw, particularly criticism from European nations.

Since October 2023, Netanyahu has cast international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as an “us vs them” moment for the country. He has frequently framed Israel as alone in a hostile world and that he is the only leader strong enough to stand up to the country’s critics.

After the United Kingdom’s Foreign Minister Ed Miliband described E1 as an “unacceptable and destructive act”, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar criticised the “patronising tone” of his statement.

With the election approaching, the way ministers respond to the E1 project could determine their political futures.

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has been one of the key proponents of E1 and could benefit from an uptick in support from right-wing Israelis over the proposed illegal settlement. His Religious Zionist Party is currently unlikely to pass the electoral threshold to even run in this year’s election.

“It’s Smotrich, he’s hyping up everything under his watch ahead of the election,” Israeli analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera from Berlin, Germany.

The fact that the government’s call for tenders to construct E1 falls so close to Israel’s election is not a coincidence, Flaschenberg said. Neither is the dramatic increase in settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where Smotrich has administrative control.

“Both he and even Netanyahu are benefitting from the outrage. Little of this is accidental,” the analyst added.

Condemnation of the E1 settlement has been almost universal. On Friday, the foreign ministers of Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates rejected the E1 settlement, calling for “immediate action to halt the E1 settlement plan”.

Earlier in the week, 15 European and North American leaders, including those from Israel’s traditional allies the United Kingdom, France and Germany, condemned the settlement.

In a joint letter , they said E1 would “undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank”. Some have pointed out that their failure to present any penalties if Israel goes ahead with the plan makes their criticism moot.

The United States has not criticised E1 itself, but did on Friday state its opposition to Israel’s annexation of the West Bank, which the illegal settlement could effectively result in.

“As the president has clearly stated, the US does not support Israel annexing the West Bank. A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region,” read a statement from the US Department of State.

So, is this really the end of the two-state solution?

Announcing plans for construction in August 2025, Smotrich had boasted that the new settlement would bury the “idea of a Palestinian state”.

Given that thousands of Palestinian homes have been demolished by Israel since its occupation of the West Bank began in 1967, some hope the same could happen to the illegal Israeli settlements that replaced them, if the two-state solution becomes a reality.

“The idea that this is irreversible is just nonsense. Every time there’s a new illegal settlement, voices in the West say that this is the end of the two-state solution,” Flaschenberg said.

“It definitely makes it less likely, but why the end? Every illegal settlement that’s been built can be demolished … why do we have to accept their presence as fact?”

Political analyst Ori Goldberg noted that the tender for the E1 settlement project came at a time Israel faced further international criticism for bombing an airfield in Syria and described the issuing of the tender as “a deliberate provocation”.

Thousands of Palestinians, most of them Bedouin, have already suffered home demolitions, displacement and restrictions on basic services as Israel expands its road network before construction in the occupied West Bank.

In April 2026, 23 Palestinians, including 15 children, were displaced from the az-Za’im Bedouin community following demolitions by the Israeli army.

The UN warns that the planned expansion of Israeli illegal settlements and associated infrastructure threatens to fragment the occupied West Bank and could forcibly displace the 18 Palestinian communities that have lived within the territory Israel now claims for decades.

articles.title: I have eight kids. Here's why the 'back-to-school' mom memes break my heart
articles.summary: A mom of eight shares why back-to-school memes celebrating kids leaving may send the wrong message to children who notice more than we think.
articles.body: Summer is the best season. My kids have no school commitments and our time is spent getting together with friends, doing weekend trips, camping, going to the lake, and enjoying the time we have with each other. My oldest is already in college so I know the feeling of time slipping through my fingers as my kids get older and create lives of their own. Time with my husband and eight children is my most precious gift and while back-to-school season is exciting, it’s certainly bittersweet. The joy of watching my kids grow into the next stage of life is balanced out by the feeling that most of August is the Sunday before school starts. Raising kids is hard, and it’s okay to feel a little relief when structure returns. But I think we should be thoughtful about the message our children receive in the way we celebrate. JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS Scrolling through social media this time of year brings meme after meme of parents, usually moms, who are thrilled the school year is starting because it’s time to ship their kids off to someone else five days a week. The photos of moms in robes on their doorstep holding a glass of wine are everywhere. Kids notice when we seem overly eager to send them away. articles.body: In 1900, financier J P Morgan bought 117 acres in Maine, including Sand Beach and Great Head, as a wedding gift for his daughter Louisa. The land is now part of Acadia National Park.The land around Great Head and Sand Beach was connected to Louisa and and her husband Herbert Satterlee for decades before it became a public property. According to National Park Service, the familyâs summer property was commonly known as 'Satterlee field'.The 117 acres purchased by financier J P Morgan included Sand Beach and Great Head. Louisa married Herbert Satterlee in New York City in November 1900. The couple later made the coastal property part of their familyâs summer life.Louisa and Herbert had two daughters, Mabel, born in 1901, and Eleanor, born in 1905. The two girls grew up exploring the landscape around their familyâs property.The story of Satterlee FieldAlthough J P Morgan purchased the land in 1900, the transaction was not formally completed until 1910 because of title issues.Before the property eventually became part of the Satterlee familyâs estate, the family already had a connection with Acadia National Park because large sections of park land bordered Satterlee Field. The Satterlees also allowed park visitors to explore Sand Beach while the land was still associated with the family.The familyâs time at the summer estate came to an end after the deaths of Louisa and Herbert. Louisa died in October 1946, while Herbert died in July 1947.A few months later, the area was hit by the October Fire of 1947. Much of the Satterlee estate was destroyed in the fire. After the fire, the familyâs connection to the land changed. Eleanor and Mabel decided to donate the property so that other people could continue to visit and enjoy the landscape that had been important to their family.How family estate became public landEleanor Morgan Satterlee, Louisa and Herbertâs daughter and J P Morganâs granddaughter, inherited the tract after her parents died. By the late 1940s, Eleanorâs health had also begun to decline.These circumstances, along with the damage caused by the 1947 fire, led Eleanor to donate the land to Acadia National Park in 1949. The donation included the area around Great Head, including Sand Beach.The National Park Service records that Eleanor donated approximately 100 acres to the United States in memory of her mother, Louisa P Satterlee.A bronze plaque near the top of the staircase leading down to Sand Beach marks the donation. It carries the following inscription- âSatterlee Field, of approximately 100 acres, was donated in 1949 by Eleanor Morgan Satterlee to the United States of America in memory of her mother, Louisa P. Satterlee, as part of Acadia National Park.âThe landscape todayThe property includes the sandy beach, reached by a staircase, and the stretch of land known as the Headlands. The National Park Service describes the landscape in terms of a human body, with the coastline forming the 'shoulders' and the projecting land resembling a 'head'.The area can now be explored by visitors through the Great Head Trail. articles.title: Scottish National Investment Bank makes 'painful' Â£138m net loss
articles.summary: The publicly-owned body, which operates independently, has invested in several firms that collapsed last year.
articles.body:
The Scottish National Investment Bank has revealed it made a net loss of Â£138m last year.

The state-owned body cited the collapse of three of its early investments - including its first, Glasgow-based laser company M Squared.

However, the bank also generated an income of Â£32m, comfortably covering its operating costs of Â£20m.

Chairman Willie Watt called the losses "painful" but said the bank had learned lessons.

The Scottish National Investment Bank, which is independent from government, was set up by ministers in 2020 with a mission to fund business and innovation to boost economic growth.

Its report for the 2025-26 financial year , external revealed a net loss of Â£138m, including Â£65m of realised losses from the failure of three early investments - M Squared Lasers, the electric car charging firm Trojan Energy and the satellite and digital company Krucial.

There was a further Â£85m of unrealised losses after rocket manufacturer Orbex and medical technology firm Pneumowave entered administration.

The bank also invested a record Â£374m in Scottish ventures, while its operating costs were below budget.

Watt said: "The realised and unrealised losses we have seen in this financial year reflect that and are not where we want to be.

"While these figures are painful for the bank, they are particularly so for the businesses which failed and of course for their teams."

He cited a tough economic environment with "tighter financial conditions, cautious sentiment and more challenging fundraising".

Watt added: "We have learned a lot over the past five years and continue to improve and tighten our investment processes along with stricter criteria for potential investments as set out in our investment strategy."

Chief executive David Ritchie called the losses "regrettable and disappointing", but said he was determined to demonstrate that a "commercially disciplined development bank can deliver for Scotland".

Which companies backed by the bank have folded?

M Squared Lasers - the Glasgow technology firm was hailed by Nicola Sturgeon as "a great example of the ambitious and innovative companies we have here in Scotland" when the national investment bank was launched in 2020. It went into administration in 2025 with debts of Â£64m

Trojan Energy - the Aberdeen-based electric vehicle charging firm collapsed into administration with debt of almost Â£30m last year

Krucial - the Glasgow-based start-up, which specialised in satellite technology, folded last year.

Orbex - set up to run a planned satellite launch facility in the north-west Highlands, the company is to be liquidated and its assets sold off

Pneumowave - headquartered in Glasgow, the medical tech firm appointed liquidators in July

Since being set up in 2020, the bank has investment more than Â£1.2bn in 53 ventures and helped to raise Â£1.9bn in third-party investment.

An independent report by Sir John Elvidge , external , a former chief civil servant to the Scottish government, found that the bank was expected to have made losses of about Â£110m by the end of 2025-26 financial year.

He said it was important that the bank learned lessons from the losses, but did not say the scale of the failed investments were necessarily higher than should be expected for a newly launched body.

Responding to the bank's annual report, First Minister John Swinney said it must be able to take risks to deliver "greater economic returns".

He said that principle was essential to "constructing an economy that is fit for the 21st Century".

Scottish Labour economy spokesperson Daniel Johnson said: "These losses must be examined and the bank's leadership must continue to work to identify investment opportunities that will deliver for our economy and our communities."

Kim Schmulian, Reform UK Scotland's finance spokesperson, said: "This is yet another example of SNP ministers gambling with taxpayers' money while those responsible try to dress up failure as a 'challenging environment'."

Scottish Conservative finance spokesman Craig Hoy said that the bank "must not become another SNP vanity project where taxpayers are left to foot the bill for failure while ministers dodge responsibility".

articles.title: Why nuclear energy is making a global comeback
articles.summary: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News.
articles.body: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News. Energy security concerns augmented by recent years of war in Ukraine and the Middle East have fueled a global resurgence of nuclear energy. In Asia, Europe, and elsewhere, governments are looking to nuclear energy as a stable power source in the face of geopolitical uncertainty, increasing electricity demand, and accelerating climate change. This includes the United States, which recently signed a thirty-year civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, though it has yet to go into effect. This resurgence marks a stunning reversal. Nuclear power development stalled after high-profile accidents such as the 1979 Three Mile Island meltdown and the 1986 Chernobyl disaster fueled public fears of the technology.

articles.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
articles.summary: His comments come as the government urged TikTok and other social media firms to remove wrong-way driving videos.
articles.body:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv, Burnham said the people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are "doing something that's truly reprehensible".

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.

It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.

The BBC has also contacted X for comment.

On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.

At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".

He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.

"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."

The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.

A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".

They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

articles.title: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
articles.summary: Business owners in both countries are navigating uncertainty and worry as the tit-for-tat import taxes ratchet up.
articles.body:
Cindy Baldassi relies on American buyers to keep her stone-and-glass jewellery company going.

Some 75% of sales of pieces including amethyst, sea glass and agates from her business, CindyLouWho2, based in Calgary, Alberta, come from Americans.

But after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed over the weekend and leaders of both countries pledged to slap 50% tariffs on each other's products, business owners on both sides of the border are bracing for the fallout.

With a majority of the items she sells falling under US President Donald Trump's newly imposed tariffs, Baldassi says she will need to add 50% to the price of most of her products to stay afloat.

"It's quite likely that it will wipe out most of my US sales," Baldassi told the BBC. "I expect that at least half of my business will be gone."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged levies starting on 8 September on US steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Trump tariffs went into effect on Saturday, hitting Canadian wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

In Canada, it is not clear how much more severe the impacts will be, since the country has grown somewhat used to the on-again-off-again trade war.

Lind Furniture has been in business for almost 60 years in the Canadian province of Ontario, selling leather furniture to big store clients like Sears and Costco over the years.

Sales dropped when Trump took office in 2025. "As soon as there were tariffs in the air, people put purchases on hold," Michael Saifer, general manager of Lind Furniture, told the BBC.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Now, his concern centres around Canadians' chances for victory.

"Everyone wants to sell to the Americans - they can buy from whoever they want," he said. "I don't know that we're going to win a war with them; we may get killed."

The US tariffs that took effect after talks broke off on Friday apply to about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian exports to the US - about 5% of what Canada ships to the US annually. The levies add to US tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

Canada would be very exposed if the import taxes multiply on both sides because 70% of its exports are to the US.

Navigating what comes next as both sides are dug in is proving a delicate balance for some business owners.

Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores.

Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff.

"If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said.

He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go.

"There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US.

"Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this."

'It's going to get worse before it gets better'

The impacts are not only being felt north of the US-Canada border. Carney promised his tariffs hitting US products in September will match Trump's "dollar-for-dollar". Details of the countermeasures will be released in the coming days, he said.

For Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing, a clothing store in Portland, Oregon, that means preparing for one of their best-selling items to potentially increase sizably in price.

Osgood creates designs that she has a Montreal-based company transfer onto pillows the couple sells in their store.

Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC.

"Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said.

The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said.

While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies.

Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol.

He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to.

"The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.

And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border.

The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state.

The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric".

"We completely understood that," she said.

But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat.

And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear.

"It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."

"Everyone wants to sell to the Americans - they can buy from whoever they want," he said. "I don't know that we're going to win a war with them; we may get killed."

The US tariffs that took effect after talks broke off on Friday apply to about $20bn (Â£15bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian exports to the US - about 5% of what Canada ships to the US annually. The levies add to US tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

Canada would be very exposed if the import taxes multiply on both sides because 70% of its exports are to the US.

Navigating what comes next as both sides are dug in is proving a delicate balance for some business owners.

Like many retailers, Matteo Sgaramella, founder of Toronto-based menswear brand Outclass, told the BBC that his company collects orders from clothing designers months before they are due to arrive in stores.

Products that US stores ordered in January will arrive in September but now with a new tariff.

"If I contact them now and tell them, hey, you know, you may get an extra 50% bill from UPS on top of what you need to pay me for this shipment, they're all going to say, 'no way, don't ship it,'" Sgaramella said.

He still has to figure out where that additional cost will go.

"There's going to be a lot of people that go out of business because of this," Sgaramella said, but noted that only 20% of his wholesale sales and 20% of his e-commerce come from the US.

"Big business can, you know, always find a way... but small businesses are going to get smashed by this."

'It's going to get worse before it gets better'

The impacts are not only being felt north of the US-Canada border. Carney promised his tariffs hitting US products in September will match Trump's "dollar-for-dollar". Details of the countermeasures will be released in the coming days, he said.

For Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing, a clothing store in Portland, Oregon, that means preparing for one of their best-selling items to potentially increase sizably in price.

Osgood creates designs that she has a Montreal-based company transfer onto pillows the couple sells in their store.

Those pillows are their best-selling gift item, retailing at $59. With the newly imposed tariffs, a normal markup would bring the price of that pillow to somewhere between $86 and $90, Osgood told the BBC.

"Gift items are really price-point sensitive; people have in their mind what they're going to pay for a gift, and they're not going to pay more than that," Roach said.

The couple, whose shop has been operating for 51 years, say they will likely hold the original price and hope the "tariff problem," as Roach calls it, gets worked out.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice; that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors, but when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck," he said.

While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies.

Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol.

He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to.

"The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.

And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border.

The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state.

The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric".

"We completely understood that," she said.

But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat.

And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear.

"It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."

articles.title: US military says strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat kills two
articles.summary: US Southern Command says Sunday’s strike targeted vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes.
articles.body:
The United States military said it struck a suspected drug-trafficking boat in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people.

In a Monday post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said Sunday’s strike targeted a vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific.

“Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking,” SOUTHCOM added.

“This operation is a clear and decisive reminder that SOUTHCOM is taking the fight directly to the cartels.”

Grainy, black-and-white video accompanying the post appeared to show a boat moving through the water immediately before a large explosion.

The post stated that under the direction of SOUTHCOM Commander General Francis L. Donovan, the Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on the low-profile vessel.

“We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists — disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” Donovan was quoted as saying.

“Let me be clear, we will not permit narco-terrorists to operate with impunity in the Western Hemisphere, nor will we allow their deadly poison to reach American communities. This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the U.S. homeland.”

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in early September, with President Donald Trump arguing that Washington is effectively at war with Latin American drug cartels.

Since then, more than 200 people have been killed in strikes across the Eastern Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, according to a tally by the AFP news agency.

However, the Trump administration has not provided definitive evidence that the targeted vessels were involved in drug trafficking.

Legal experts and rights groups warn that the attacks could amount to extrajudicial killings.

The Pentagon’s inspector general said in May that it would review whether the military followed standard targeting procedures, though the evaluation will not examine the legal authority behind the strikes.
